study_identification_part.si4_title: Mapping cerebellar anatomical heterogeneity in mental and neurological illnesses

study_characteristics_part.sc1_study_objective: To map the normative development and aging of the cerebellum across the lifespan at high spatial precision, and to apply these normative models to investigate cerebellar heterogeneity in five clinical illnesses (autism spectrum disorder, mild cognitive impairment, Alzheimer disease, bipolar disorder, and schizophrenia).

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: Group comparisons of z-scores between clinical and control groups were performed using Mann-Whitney U tests with Bonferroni correction. Associations between the percentage of extreme deviations and cognitive/symptom scores were tested using Spearman correlation analyses, with P values corrected for multiple comparisons.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: The study provides voxel-wise normative models of the cerebellum across the lifespan, revealing significant but heterogeneous structural deviations in individuals with ASD, MCI, AD, and SZ, with these deviations being associated with cognitive scores.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: Using a reference cohort of >54,000 individuals, this study created high-resolution normative models of cerebellar anatomy. Application to clinical groups revealed that individuals with SZ and AD showed predominantly negative deviations (smaller volumes), while ASD and MCI showed both extreme positive and negative deviations. These deviations were highly heterogeneous, with only small percentages of individuals within a diagnosis showing spatial overlap. Voxel-wise deviations were aggregated using anatomical and functional atlases, showing significant group differences in deviation patterns. For example, in ASD, extreme negative deviations were prominent in a region linked to the dorsal attention network. Furthermore, the percentage of extreme deviations was correlated with cognitive measures, such as a positive correlation between positive deviations and PIQ in ASD, and correlations between deviations and full-scale IQ in SZ.

caa10_key_limitations.answer: Limitations include the lack of detailed and harmonized behavioral, cognitive, genetic, and medical history data across the aggregated datasets; low coverage in the normative models for very young ages and the 30-40 age range; limited generalizability due to the dataset primarily representing Western/European populations; and the cross-sectional design preventing analysis of treatment effects.
caa10_key_limitations.supporting_text: First, we lack coherent and detailed behavioral, cognitive, genetic, phenotypic, and medical history information... In addition, the coverages of lifespan normative models in the very young age and in the age range of 30-40 years were relatively low... Due to limited availability regarding ethnicity information, this paper represents primarily western populations... This paper focuses on large-baseline cross-sectional data, which limits the examination of the effects of drugs or treatment.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: The study demonstrates a novel application of voxel-wise normative models by projecting individual deviation maps onto multiple existing cerebellar atlases (anatomical, task-based functional, and resting-state functional), allowing for enhanced functional interpretation of structural deviations.

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: The study provides extensive supplementary materials, including detailed lifespan trajectory plots for all 28 cerebellar lobules (Supplementary Fig. 2) and evaluation metrics for the normative models (Supplementary Fig. 1). Several sensitivity analyses were conducted, including repeating the main analyses on age-, sex-, and scanning-site-matched control groups (Supplementary Fig. 6), which yielded similar but statistically weaker effects. The authors also performed exploratory analyses on the effect of ethnicity (finding similar patterns in the European subsample, Supplementary Fig. 7) and medication load in schizophrenia (finding no significant associations). Subgroup analyses within ASD (Asperger's vs. Autism) were also performed (Supplementary Fig. 8).
